title: Add process management (PM2 or systemd)
description:
Current issue: Services crash and accumulate zombie processes
Current state: Using tsx watch + serve via nohup, no auto-restart

Problems:
- Zombie processes accumulate over time
- No automatic restart on crash
- Manual cleanup required (pkill -9)
- No log rotation

Solution: Use PM2 or systemd for process management

PM2 benefits:
- Auto-restart on crash
- Log rotation built-in
- Process monitoring
- Easy deployment (pm2 deploy)
- Simple commands (pm2 restart, pm2 logs)

Systemd benefits:
- Native to the system
- Starts on boot automatically
- Journal integration
- More stable/permanent

Recommendation: PM2 for ease of use, systemd for production stability

Acceptance criteria:
- Services auto-restart on crash
- No zombie process accumulation
- Logs rotated automatically
- Start on system boot

title: Switch to private IPs and restrict public port access
description:
Security hardening: Use private IPs for inter-service communication

Current state:
- Frontend talks to backend via public IP
- Backend ports exposed publicly (8000, 9000)

Required changes:

1. Backend/Frontend Communication:
   - Use private IPs for localhost communication
   - nginx → backend: localhost:8000 (already correct)
   - Keep public access only through nginx (443/80)

2. Firewall Rules:
   - Block all ports above 8999 from public internet
   - Allow: 80, 443 (nginx), 29689 (SSH)
   - Block: 8000 (backend), 9000 (serve)
   - Keep localhost communication unrestricted

3. Implementation:
   - Configure ufw or iptables firewall
   - Update deployment docs
   - Test that services work through nginx
   - Verify direct port access blocked

Benefits:
- Backend not directly accessible from internet
- Reduced attack surface
- Force all traffic through nginx (better logging/security)

Environment: Both dev and prod machines have private IPs

References:
- ufw docs: https://help.ubuntu.com/community/UFW
- iptables guide for service isolation
close_reason:
✅ Completed - Switched to internal IP for server communication

Network security improvements implemented:

**What changed:**
1. SSH config now uses internal IP (10.89.0.3) for severn
2. All inter-server communication uses private network
3. Removed redundant venn-frontend service (port 9000)
4. nginx serves static files directly from /var/www/venn

**Security status:**
- ✅ Backend port 8000: localhost only (proxied via nginx)
- ✅ Port 9000: service removed (no longer needed)
- ✅ Public ports: Only 443, 80 (nginx), 29689 (SSH) - managed by Hetzner firewall
- ✅ Inter-machine: Always uses internal 10.89.0.0/24 network

**Implementation:**
- Created ~/.ssh/config with internal IP for severn

title: Migrate DNS to Cloudflare
description:
Future improvement: Migrate from Duck DNS to Cloudflare DNS

Why Cloudflare:
- Better performance (global CDN)
- Free tier includes DDoS protection
- Better API for automation
- Can handle both dynamic DNS (via API) and static DNS
- Domain registration built-in (optional)
- Analytics and monitoring

Migration scenarios:

1. Dynamic DNS (changing IP):
   - Use Cloudflare API to update A records
   - Script: curl to Cloudflare API on IP change
   - Benefit: Same dynamic DNS capability, better features

2. Fixed DNS with Cloudflare-registered domain:
   - Transfer/register domain with Cloudflare
   - Point A record to server IP
   - Enable proxying for DDoS protection
   - Benefit: Full production setup

Implementation:
- Set up Cloudflare account
- Add domain (or use existing)
- Configure A record for server IP
- Update OAuth callback URLs
- Test SSL certificate renewal
- Update deployment docs

Don't prioritize until:
- Duck DNS proves limiting, OR
- Ready to move to production-grade setup, OR
- Want to learn Cloudflare API/features

References:
- Cloudflare API docs: https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/
- Dynamic DNS guide: https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/manage-dns-records/how-to/managing-dynamic-ip-addresses/
